claim: Apolipoprotein A1 (apoA1) is the major protein component of high-density lipoprotein (HDL).
source: Apolipoprotein A1 (apoA1) is the major protein component of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and has well documented anti-inflammatory properties.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background information.

claim: ApoA1 has well documented anti-inflammatory properties.
source: Apolipoprotein A1 (apoA1) is the major protein component of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and has well documented anti-inflammatory properties.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Acute (20–60 min) apoA1 treatment induced a substantial (50–90%) reduction in macrophage chemotaxis to a range of chemoattractants.
source: Acute (20–60 min) apoA1 treatment induced a substantial (50–90%) reduction in macrophage chemotaxis to a range of chemoattractants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Acute apoA1 treatment was anti-inflammatory in vivo as shown by pre-treatment of monocytes prior to adoptive transfer into an on-going murine peritonitis model.
source: This acute treatment was anti-inflammatory in vivo as shown by pre-treatment of monocytes prior to adoptive transfer into an on-going murine peritonitis model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: ApoA1 rapidly disrupts membrane lipid rafts.
source: We find that apoA1 rapidly disrupts membrane lipid rafts, and as a consequence, dampens the PI3K/Akt signalling pathway that coordinates reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: ApoA1 dampens the PI3K/Akt signalling pathway that coordinates reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and cell migration.
source: We find that apoA1 rapidly disrupts membrane lipid rafts, and as a consequence, dampens the PI3K/Akt signalling pathway that coordinates reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CC chemokines mediate leukocyte trafficking in immune homeostasis.
source: CC chemokines are low-molecular-weight signalling proteins that mediate leukocyte trafficking in immune homeostasis and play a non-redundant role in monocyte/macrophage recruitment in pre-clinical models of inflammation (Charo and Ransohoff, 2006; Mackay, 2008; White et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CC chemokines play a non-redundant role in monocyte/macrophage recruitment in pre-clinical models of inflammation.
source: CC chemokines are low-molecular-weight signalling proteins that mediate leukocyte trafficking in immune homeostasis and play a non-redundant role in monocyte/macrophage recruitment in pre-clinical models of inflammation (Charo and Ransohoff, 2006; Mackay, 2008; White et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrophage chemotaxis towards CC chemokines and other pathophysiological chemoattractants are mediated by Gi/o coupled G protein coupled receptors.
source: Macrophage chemotaxis towards CC chemokines and other pathophysiological chemoattractants, such as N-formylmethionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine (fMLF), complement component 5a (C5a) and chemerin, are mediated by Gi/o coupled G protein coupled receptors (Allen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Chemokine-mediated recruitment of monocytes and macrophages are attractive areas for the development of novel anti-inflammatory agents.
source: Chemokine-mediated recruitment of monocytes and macrophages, in addition to retention and activation, are attractive areas for the development of novel anti-inflammatory agents that could find application in a wide range of chronic inflammatory pathologies (Asquith et al., 2015; Schall and Proudfoot, 2011; Tabas and Glass, 2013; Zernecke and Weber, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ApoA1 is widely recognized to have atheroprotective properties.
source: Apolipoprotein A1 (apoA1) is the major structural protein of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and is widely recognized to have atheroprotective properties (Fisher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The cellular mechanisms that account for the observed anti-inflammatory effects of apoA1 and HDL are incompletely understood.
source: The cellular mechanisms that account for the observed anti-inflammatory effects of apoA1 and HDL, including those on innate immune cell activation, are incompletely understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Chronic treatment of human monocytes with HDL and apoA1 has been reported to reduce chemotaxis to fMLF.
source: Chronic treatment of human monocytes with HDL and apoA1 has been reported to reduce chemotaxis to fMLF (Diederich et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Acute exposure to apoA1 (40 µg/ml for 60 min) reduced biogel elicited murine macrophage chemotaxis to CCL2 by 67%.
source: Biogel elicited murine macrophages (4 × 105/well) were pre-treated with apoA1 (40 µg/ml; a standard amount used in cholesterol efflux studies, e.g.Adorni et al., 2007) for 60 min at 37°C, 5% CO2 and allowed to migrate towards 10 nM CCL2. The representative trace in Figure 1A shows a clear reduction in chemotaxis towards CCL2 as quantified by slope and max-min analysis (67% reduction, p≤0.01, Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Acute exposure to apoA1 (40 µg/ml for 60 min) reduced biogel elicited murine macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 by 71%.
source: A similar reduction in chemotaxis (71% reduction, p≤0.01) was observed in response to 10 nM CCL5 (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Acute exposure to apoA1 (40 µg/ml for 60 min) reduced biogel elicited murine macrophage chemotaxis to C5a by 52%.
source: a 52% reduction in macrophage chemotaxis was observed in response to 10 nM C5a peptide (p≤0.05, Figure 1G–I)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Acute exposure to apoA1 (40 µg/ml for 60 min) reduced biogel elicited murine macrophage chemotaxis to chemerin by 80%.
source: and a 80% reduction in chemotaxis to 10 nM chemerin, a potent chemoattractant of antigen presenting cells (p≤0.01, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Washing cells following acute exposure to apoA1 led to a similar impairment in migration as unwashed cells.
source: We also found that washing cells following acute exposure to apoA1 led to a similar impairment in migration as unwashed cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation, though the data is not shown.

claim: Macrophage migration towards CCL5 was significantly impaired when cells were pre-treated with apoA1 as determined by the forward migration index.
source: Analysis revealed that macrophage migration towards CCL5 was significantly impaired (p≤0.05) when cells were pre-treated with apoA1 as determined by the forward migration index (FMI) −0.090 v −0.012, (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 1J-M.

claim: Treatment with apoA1 reduced the Euclidean distance and velocity of CCL5-stimulated macrophages to that of unstimulated controls.
source: Furthermore, treatment with apoA1 reduced the Euclidean distance and velocity of CCL5-stimulated macrophages to that of unstimulated controls, demonstrating a loss in cell directionality.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Both 20 min and 40 min pre-treatment with apoA1 significantly reduced macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 by 75–86%.
source: Comparable to 60 min pre-treatment, both 20 min and 40 min were shown to significantly (p≤0.001) reduce macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 by 75–86% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Pre-treatment with 20 or 80 µg/ml of apoA1 for 60 min reduced macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 by 43% and 51% respectively.
source: Pre-treatment with 20 or 80 µg/ml of apoA1 for 60 min was also shown to reduce macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 by 43% and 51% (p≤0.05), respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: ApoA1 functions in the first step of reverse cholesterol transport, cholesterol efflux from macrophages, through both ABCA1-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
source: ApoA1 functions in the first step of reverse cholesterol transport, cholesterol efflux from macrophages, through both ABCA1-dependent and -independent mechanisms (Phillips, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The migration capacity of macrophages to CCL5 treated with either recombinant wild-type apoA1 (rapoA1) or 5-OH-Trp72 rapoA1 (ox-rapoA1) was significantly inhibited by 90–94%.
source: Notably, the migration capacity of macrophages to CCL5 treated with either recombinant wild-type apoA1 (rapoA1) or 5-OH-Trp72 rapoA1 (ox-rapoA1) was significantly inhibited (90–94% reduction, p≤0.001) (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Macrophages from both C57BL/6 and Abca1-/- mice have an equal capacity to migrate to CCL5.
source: We found that macrophages from both C57BL/6 and Abca1-/- mice have an equal capacity to migrate to CCL5 (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Migration of macrophages from both C57BL/6 and Abca1-/- mice is inhibited by 62–70% following treatment with apoA1 for 60 min.
source: and that migration of both is inhibited by 62–70% (p≤0.05–0.001) following treatment with apoA1 for 60 min (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: Treatment of macrophages with methyl β-cyclodextrin (CyD) led to markedly reduced macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 by 91%.
source: Treatment of macrophages with the non-specific cholesterol depleting agent methyl β-cyclodextrin (CyD) also led to markedly reduced macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 (91% (p≤0.001); Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G–I.

claim: The inhibitory effect of apoA1 on macrophage chemotaxis is mediated through a cholesterol-efflux pathway, independent of ABCA1.
source: Taken together, these results support a role for the contribution of a cholesterol-efflux pathway, independent of ABCA1, mediating the inhibitory effect of apoA1 on macrophage chemotaxis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that ox-rapoA1 and Abca1-/- macrophages respond similarly to apoA1 treatment.

claim: Acute apoA1 treatment reduced human monocyte chemotaxis to CCL2 by 43%.
source: Slope (Figure 3B) and max-min analysis (Figure 3C) of monocytes from multiple donors confirmed a significant 43% reduction in chemotaxis (p≤0.05) towards CCL2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Acute apoA1 treatment reduced human monocyte chemotaxis to CCL5 by 50%.
source: A similar significant inhibition in monocyte migration (p≤0.05) was also observed in response to CCL5 (50% reduction) and C5a (42% reduction) (Figure 3D–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Acute apoA1 treatment reduced human monocyte chemotaxis to C5a by 42%.
source: A similar significant inhibition in monocyte migration (p≤0.05) was also observed in response to CCL5 (50% reduction) and C5a (42% reduction) (Figure 3D–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Human monocyte migration towards CCL5 was significantly impaired when cells were pre-treated with apoA1 as determined by the forward migration index.
source: A similar degree of inhibition was observed with the ibidi chamber assay, with the human monocyte migration towards CCL5 significantly impaired (p≤0.01) when cells were pre-treated with apoA1 (representative traces shown in Figure 3J–L) as determined by the forward migration index (FMI) −0.246 v 0.064, (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J-M.

claim: Treatment with apoA1 significantly reduced the Euclidean distance, total distance, velocity and directionality of CCL5-stimulated human monocytes.
source: Furthermore, treatment with apoA1 significantly reduced the Euclidean distance, total distance, velocity and directionality of CCL5-stimulated human monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Pre-incubation of PBMCs with apoA1 considerably reduced cell capture in flow chamber assays.
source: Pre-incubation of PBMCs with apoA1 considerably reduced cell capture as shown in the representative images (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PBMC rolling, adhesion and transmigration were all significantly reduced by 20–45% following pre-treatment with apoA1 for 45 min.
source: PBMC rolling, adhesion and transmigration were all significantly reduced by 20–45% following pre-treatment with apoA1 for 45 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: No differences were observed in the expression of active CD11b, total CD11b, CD49b, CD62L and C5aR1 on human monocytes following apoA1 treatment and C5a stimulation.
source: No differences were observed in the expression of any of these markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–J) indicating that the effects of acute apoA1 treatment were independent of receptor and adhesion molecule modulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–J.

claim: The effects of acute apoA1 treatment were independent of receptor and adhesion molecule modulation.
source: No differences were observed in the expression of any of these markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–J) indicating that the effects of acute apoA1 treatment were independent of receptor and adhesion molecule modulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that receptor and adhesion molecule expression was unchanged.

claim: Acute pre-treatment with apoA1 ex vivo reduced GFP+ monocyte recruitment to the peritoneal cavity of recipient mice by 65%.
source: Acute pre-treatment with apoA1 ex vivo reduced GFP+monocyte recruitment to the peritoneal cavity of recipient mice by 65% (p≤0.01) when compared to vehicle treated cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Similar levels of GFP+ monocytes were present in the blood of mice that received adoptively transferred apoA1 or vehicle treated monocytes.
source: This occurred despite similar levels of GFP+ monocytes in the blood of mice that received adoptively transferred apoA1 or vehicle treated monocytes (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Total monocytes recruited to the peritoneal cavity and circulating in the blood were equivalent at 16 hr in all groups of recipient mice following zymosan challenge.
source: Importantly, total monocytes recruited to the peritoneal cavity and circulating in the blood were equivalent at 16 hr in all groups of recipient mice following zymosan challenge (Figure 4D and F), highlighting that the effects of treatment were restricted to only the monocytes pre-treated with apoA1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: The effects of apoA1 treatment were restricted to only the monocytes pre-treated with apoA1.
source: Importantly, total monocytes recruited to the peritoneal cavity and circulating in the blood were equivalent at 16 hr in all groups of recipient mice following zymosan challenge (Figure 4D and F), highlighting that the effects of treatment were restricted to only the monocytes pre-treated with apoA1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only pre-treated monocytes showed reduced recruitment.

claim: Total cell recruitment in Apoa1Tg mice was significantly reduced by 27% compared to C57BL/6 controls in zymosan-induced peritonitis.
source: Total cell recruitment in Apoa1Tg mice was significantly reduced by 27% (p≤0.05) when compared to C57BL/6 controls, with a reduction in total neutrophils (26%, p≤0.05) and monocytes (30%, p≤0.01) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Total neutrophil recruitment in Apoa1Tg mice was reduced by 26% compared to C57BL/6 controls in zymosan-induced peritonitis.
source: Total cell recruitment in Apoa1Tg mice was significantly reduced by 27% (p≤0.05) when compared to C57BL/6 controls, with a reduction in total neutrophils (26%, p≤0.05) and monocytes (30%, p≤0.01) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Total monocyte recruitment in Apoa1Tg mice was reduced by 30% compared to C57BL/6 controls in zymosan-induced peritonitis.
source: Total cell recruitment in Apoa1Tg mice was significantly reduced by 27% (p≤0.05) when compared to C57BL/6 controls, with a reduction in total neutrophils (26%, p≤0.05) and monocytes (30%, p≤0.01) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Elevated apoA1 levels significantly suppressed the recruitment of the Ly6Chi monocyte subset to peritoneal cavity by 42%.
source: Elevated apoA1 levels significantly suppressed the recruitment of the Ly6Chi monocyte subset to peritoneal cavity (42%, p≤0.05, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: No changes in Ly6Clo subset or in total blood white cell counts were observed between Apoa1Tg and control mice.
source: No changes in Ly6Clo subset or in total blood white cell counts were observed between any of the experimental groups (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F–G.

claim: No significant differences in chemokines CCL2 and CXCL1 were observed in peritoneal exudates between Apoa1Tg and control mice.
source: Chemokines CCL2 and CXCL1 were measured in the peritoneal exudates of mice from the 4 hr and 16 hr time-points, but no significant differences were observed (CXCL1 was non detectable at 16 hr) (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: Similar levels of chemokines, but reduced neutrophil and monocyte influx, suggests that changes in the intrinsic properties of the leukocytes were responsible for the reduction in innate immune cell recruitment.
source: Similar levels of chemokines, but reduced neutrophil and monocyte influx, suggests that changes in the intrinsic properties of the leukocytes were responsible for the reduction in innate immune cell recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chemokine levels were unchanged but cell recruitment was reduced.

claim: Pre-treatment with apoA1 reduced Akt phosphorylation in human monocytes by 54% following C5a stimulation.
source: Pre-treatment with apoA1 reduced Akt phosphorylation by 54%, as determined by western blotting and densitometry (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A significant reduction in Akt signalling was observed following apoA1 and CyD pre-treatment of biogel elicited murine macrophages (reduction of 32% and 63% respectively).
source: A similar significant reduction in Akt signalling was also observed following apoA1 and CyD pre-treatment of biogel elicited murine macrophages (reduction of 32% and 63% respectively, Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: Pre-treatment of RAW macrophages with apoA1 for 1 hr prior to stimulation with C5a led to a reduction in PI3K activity by 36%.
source: Pre-treatment of RAW macrophages with apoA1 for 1 hr prior to stimulation with C5a led to a reduction in PI3K activity by 36% (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PI3K inhibitor studies revealed significant reduction of macrophage chemotaxis in vitro.
source: and PI3K inhibitor studies revealed significant reduction of macrophage chemotaxis in vitro (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–F.

claim: ApoA1 modulates PI3K/Akt signalling resulting in a significant impairment of monocyte and macrophage chemokine-induced migration.
source: Taken together, these results provide evidence that apoA1 modulates PI3K/Akt signalling resulting in a significant impairment of monocyte and macrophage chemokine-induced migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results showing reduced PI3K/Akt activity and reduced chemotaxis.

claim: No differences in G-protein coupled receptor 'upstream' phenomena, such as cAMP levels, Ca2+ mobilisation or β-arrestin recruitment were found as a consequence of apoA1 pre-treatment.
source: In our initial studies, we found no differences in G-protein coupled receptor 'upstream' phenomena, such as cAMP levels, Ca2+ mobilisation or β-arrestin recruitment as a consequence of apoA1 pre-treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre-treatment with apoA1, rapoA1, ox-rapoA1, or CyD led to a significant reduction in total cell caveolin-1.
source: Pre-treatment with apoA1, rapoA1, ox-rapoA1, or CyD led to a significant reduction in total cell caveolin-1 (Figure 7A–B) as determined by western blotting
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–B.

claim: Pre-treatment with apoA1, rapoA1, ox-rapoA1, or CyD led to a significant reduction in ganglioside GM1 expression.
source: Pre-treatment with apoA1, rapoA1, ox-rapoA1, or CyD led to a significant reduction in total cell caveolin-1 (Figure 7A–B) as determined by western blotting, and ganglioside GM1 expression as determined by flow cytometry (Figure 7C) or confocal fluorescence microscopy (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: Cellular free cholesterol is distributed between both low (rafts) and high (non-rafts) density fractions.
source: As previously reported (Adorni et al., 2007; Koseki et al., 2007), cellular free cholesterol is distributed between both low (rafts) and high (non-rafts) density fractions (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and experimental data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Treatment with apoA1, ox-rapoA1, or CyD leads to a significant reduction in cholesterol content in both raft and non-raft fractions.
source: Treatment with apoA1 (40 µg/ml), ox-rapoA1 (40 µg/ml), or CyD leads to a significant reduction in cholesterol content in both raft and non-raft fractions, demonstrating that apoA1 can significantly modulate the composition of this signalling nanodomain (Figure 7I–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I–J.

claim: ApoA1 can significantly modulate the composition of membrane lipid raft signalling nanodomains.
source: Treatment with apoA1 (40 µg/ml), ox-rapoA1 (40 µg/ml), or CyD leads to a significant reduction in cholesterol content in both raft and non-raft fractions, demonstrating that apoA1 can significantly modulate the composition of this signalling nanodomain (Figure 7I–J).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that apoA1 reduces cholesterol in lipid raft fractions.

claim: Diseases in which chronic inflammation is a central feature of their pathology are significant contributors to mortality and serious morbidities worldwide.
source: Diseases in which chronic inflammation is a central feature of their pathology are significant contributors to mortality and serious morbidities worldwide.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the discussion.

claim: A major factor that sustains inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases is a mobilization and activation of the innate immune system.
source: A major factor that sustains inflammation in these diseases is a mobilization and activation of the innate immune system (Tabas and Glass, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Chronic inflammation is characterized by the continued recruitment of circulating monocytes, in part mediated by their response to chemokines.
source: Chronic inflammation is characterized by the continued recruitment of circulating monocytes, in part mediated by their response to chemokines, such as CCL2 and CCL5, which are synthesized locally in response to tissue damage and resultant locally-generated inflammatory mediators (Tabas and Glass, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both HDL and its major protein component apoA1 can inhibit leukocyte chemotaxis to various chemokines.
source: It has been previously reported that both HDL and its major protein component apoA1 can inhibit leukocyte chemotaxis to various chemokines (Bursill et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Ansell et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies on apoA1 and HDL effects on chemotaxis have been heavily weighted towards experimental conditions in which the assays were exclusively performed in vitro or the duration of treatment was prolonged (≥24 hr).
source: Previous studies have been heavily weighted towards experimental conditions in which the assays were exclusively performed in vitro or the duration of treatment was prolonged (≥24 hr).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous literature.

claim: Only a short exposure (<1 hr) of monocytes or macrophages to apoA1 is required to reduce chemotaxis to chemoattractants in vitro and recruitment to an inflammatory site in vivo.
source: Our major findings are that: (1) only a short exposure (<1 hr) of monocytes or macrophages to apoA1 is required to reduce chemotaxis to chemoattractants in vitro and most notably, recruitment to an inflammatory site in vivo
evidence: This is a summary of the major findings from the experimental data presented.

claim: ApoA1 treatment reduces both the velocity and the directionality of macrophage migration to an established chemokine gradient.
source: (2) apoA1 treatment reduces both the velocity and the directionality of macrophage migration to an established chemokine gradient
evidence: This is a summary of the major findings from the experimental data presented.

claim: Inhibition of monocyte-derived cell chemotaxis by apoA1 requires cholesterol depletion of the cells, through a mechanism independent of ABCA1.
source: (3) inhibition of monocyte-derived cell chemotaxis requires cholesterol depletion of the cells, through a mechanism independent of ABCA1, a cholesterol transporter previously invoked to explain certain anti-inflammatory effects of apoA1 (Murphy et al., 2008), but rather through cholesterol efflux most likely by aqueous diffusion (Adorni et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a summary of the major findings from the experimental data presented, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: ApoA1 and CyD treatment disrupts plasma membrane lipid rafts by cholesterol depletion, which dampens the signalling pathway required for reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: We propose a model in which apoA1 and CyD treatment disrupts plasma membrane lipid rafts by cholesterol depletion, which, in turn, dampens the signalling pathway required for reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, as reflected by impaired PI3K/Akt activation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: In Bursill et al., a 24 hr treatment of monocytes with recombinant HDL resulted in reduced chemotaxis, and this was associated with decreased expression of CCR2 and CX3CR1.
source: For example, in Bursill et al., a 24 hr treatment of monocytes with recombinant HDL resulted in reduced chemotaxis, and this was associated with decreased expression of CCR2 and CX3CR1 (Bursill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Long-term effects of apoA1 on chemokine receptor expression are unlikely to be the basis for the observed ~80% reduction in macrophage chemotaxis following only 20 min of exposure to apoA1.
source: These long-term effects are unlikely to be the basis for the observed ~80% reduction in macrophage chemotaxis following only 20 min of exposure to apoA1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of long-term and short-term treatment effects.

claim: Important 'upstream' or 'receptor proximal' signalling functions of chemokine G protein–coupled receptors were not affected by acute treatment with apoA1.
source: In our experiments, important "upstream" or "receptor proximal" signalling functions of chemokine G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) were not affected by acute treatment with apoA1 i.e. decreased intracellular cAMP levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), β-arrestin recruitment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and Ca2+ flux (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Continuous exposure to apoA1 was not required for significant inhibition of chemotaxis.
source: In other words, continuous exposure to apoA1 was not required for significant inhibition of chemotaxis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that washing cells after apoA1 treatment still resulted in inhibition.

claim: Continuous and prolonged exposure of leukocytes to apoA1 and HDL, inherent to the Apoa1Tg mouse model, was associated with reduced recruitment of innate immune cells to sites of inflammation.
source: For example, continuous and prolonged exposure of leukocytes to apoA1 and HDL, inherent to the Apoa1Tg mouse model, was associated with reduced recruitment of innate immune cells to sites of inflammation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only 45 min ex-vivo exposure of monocytes to apoA1 was required to reduce their recruitment to an inflammatory site by 65%.
source: Thus, it was especially notable that in our adoptive transfer approach, only 45 min ex-vivo exposure of monocytes to apoA1 was required to reduce their recruitment to an inflammatory site by 65% (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rapidity of apoA1 effects in vitro and in vivo parallels the acute loss of lipid rafts in monocytes or macrophages.
source: That the rapidity of these effects in vitro and in vivo parallels the acute loss of lipid rafts in monocytes (Murphy et al., 2008) or macrophages (Figure 7) is not likely to be a coincidence.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation between apoA1 effects and lipid raft disruption.

claim: Rapid desensitization to the chemoattractant effects of chemokines likely represents the perturbation of lipid rafts, which are crucial to the common signalling machinery downstream from chemokine receptors.
source: Rather, this rapid desensitization to the chemoattractant effects of chemokines likely represents the perturbation of lipid rafts, which are crucial to the common signalling machinery downstream from chemokine receptors that are required for the reorganization of the cytoskeleton and integral to chemotaxis (Vorotnikov, 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Incubation with apoA1 was effective in blunting chemotaxis to multiple chemokines and chemoattractants, yet the early events following receptor ligation were unimpaired.
source: Consistent with this is our finding that incubation with apoA1 was effective in blunting chemotaxis to multiple chemokines and chemoattractants, yet the early events following receptor ligation were unimpaired (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lipid raft abundance was reduced after incubation of macrophages with apoA1.
source: More directly, we show using independent assays (western blotting and flow cytometry) that lipid raft abundance was reduced after incubation of macrophages with apoA1, as was Akt phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Akt activation in response to phosphorylation by PI3K is required for chemotaxis.
source: Akt activation in response to phosphorylation by PI3K is required for chemotaxis and was confirmed by our experiments using the PI3K inhibitor, wortmannin (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–F.

claim: Lipid rafts are enriched in cholesterol and its depletion is known to change the content and function of many of its components.
source: Lipid rafts are enriched in cholesterol and its depletion is known to change the content and function of many of its components (Simons and Toomre, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most studies of apoA1's anti-inflammatory effects have focused on cholesterol efflux mediated by specific membrane factors, in particular ABCA1.
source: While it is long been appreciated that apoA1 is a major acceptor of cellular cholesterol, and therefore can affect the lipid raft structure and functions, most studies of apoA1's anti-inflammatory effects have focused on cholesterol efflux mediated by specific membrane factors, in particular ABCA1 (e.g. Wang et al., 2001; Murphy et al., 2008; Pagler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The results are consistent with a non-specific cholesterol depletion process (aqueous diffusion) being responsible for the impairment in chemotaxis.
source: By multiple criteria, our results are consistent with a non-specific cholesterol depletion process (sometimes called aqueous diffusion (Adorni et al., 2007) that was responsible for the impairment in chemotaxis
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing ABCA1-independence and supported by a citation.

claim: Under the conditions of the assays using non-cholesterol loaded cells, ~80% of cholesterol efflux is likely through the aqueous diffusion mechanism.
source: It should be noted that under the conditions of our assays using non-cholesterol loaded cells, ~80% of cholesterol efflux is likely through the aqueous diffusion mechanism (Adorni et al., 2007), and this dominance is consistent with our results.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ApoA1 can promote cholesterol efflux in Abca1-/- macrophages.
source: Furthermore, that apoA1 can promote cholesterol efflux in Abca1-/- macrophages has also been reported (Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The inhibitory effect of apoA1 on macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 is not affected by cholesterol loading of the cell.
source: In addition, the inhibitory effect of apoA1 on macrophage chemotaxis to CCL5 is not affected by cholesterol loading of the cell (data not shown), consistent with apoA1's ability to promote cholesterol removal from membrane lipid rafts of these cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Continued monocyte recruitment and macrophage activation are hallmarks of sites of chronic inflammation.
source: Continued monocyte recruitment and macrophage activation are hallmarks of sites of chronic inflammation.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge.

claim: CC chemokines play a key role in monocyte recruitment and macrophage activation in pre-clinical models of human diseases characterised by chronic inflammation.
source: CC chemokines play a key role in monocyte recruitment and macrophage activation in pre-clinical models of human diseases characterised by chronic inflammation (Charo and Ransohoff, 2006; White et al., 2013; Tabas and Glass, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Extending the findings from chemokine receptor knockout mice to interventional studies in man using chemokine receptor antagonists has proven challenging.
source: Extending the findings from chemokine receptor knockout mice to interventional studies in man using chemokine receptor antagonists has proven challenging with multiple drugs that target single chemokine receptors failing to progress beyond early phase randomised clinical trials (Schall and Proudfoot, 2011; Koelink et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The effects of netrin on macrophage chemotaxis are dependent on the Unc5b receptor.
source: The effects of netrin on macrophage chemotaxis are dependent on the Unc5b receptor while our experiments show that the effects of apoA1 occur via a receptor-independent mechanism by changing lipid raft organisation leading to decreased PI3K activity and hence decreased monocyte/macrophage adhesion, rolling and chemotaxis.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work on netrin.

claim: The effects of apoA1 occur via a receptor-independent mechanism by changing lipid raft organisation leading to decreased PI3K activity and hence decreased monocyte/macrophage adhesion, rolling and chemotaxis.
source: The effects of netrin on macrophage chemotaxis are dependent on the Unc5b receptor while our experiments show that the effects of apoA1 occur via a receptor-independent mechanism by changing lipid raft organisation leading to decreased PI3K activity and hence decreased monocyte/macrophage adhesion, rolling and chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic findings from the experimental data.

claim: ApoA1's anti-tumorigenic activity was attributed, in part, to suppression of the recruitment and accumulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC).
source: The present results are relevant to our recent studies of apoA1's anti-tumorigenic activity (Zamanian-Daryoush et al., 2013). This effect was attributed, in part, to suppression of the recruitment and accumulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), potent stimulators of tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MDSC recruitment to tumors was significantly reduced in both apoA1 Tg mice and in apoA1-deficient mice receiving apoA1 therapy.
source: Notably, MDSC recruitment to tumors was significantly reduced in both apoA1 Tg mice and in apoA1-deficient mice receiving apoA1 therapy.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: The ability of apoA1 to suppress the recruitment of MDSCs to tumors is in agreement with current results showing the ability of apoA1 to suppress myeloid cell migration to inflammatory sites.
source: The ability of apoA1 to suppress the recruitment of MDSCs to tumors, therefore, is in agreement with our current results showing the ability of apoA1 to suppress myeloid cell migration to inflammatory sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of current and previous findings.

claim: It is likely that apoA1's ability to modulate membrane lipid raft cholesterol content influences signalling pathways regulating MDSC recruitment to tumors.
source: While the exact molecular mechanism behind apoA1's anti-tumor effect is currently unknown, given the similarities between the results in the cancer and inflammation settings, it is likely that apoA1's ability to modulate membrane lipid raft cholesterol content influences signalling pathways regulating MDSC recruitment to tumors.
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarities between the current findings and previous cancer studies.

claim: Nissen and colleagues showed regression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients given 5 weekly intravenous injections of recombinant apoA1 particles.
source: Using recombinant apoA1 particles, Nissen and colleagues showed regression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients given 5 weekly intravenous injections (Nissen et al., 2003; Kingwell et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that the efficacy of apoA1 infusions in atherosclerosis regression was due, at least in part, by the mechanisms illustrated by the current studies.
source: and it is tempting to speculate that the efficacy was due, at least in part, by the mechanisms illustrated by our studies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings.

claim: ApoA1 infusion may be therapeutic in clinical situations where reduced monocyte recruitment to sites of inflammation would be beneficial.
source: Our in vivo findings (Figures 4, 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) suggest that apoA1 infusion may also be therapeutic in other clinical situations where reduced monocyte recruitment to sites of inflammation would be beneficial.
evidence: This is speculation based on the in vivo findings.

claim: Limiting the initial rush of inflammatory leukocytes into sites of injury could have a significant effect on subsequent tissue injury and repair processes in ischemia reperfusion injury, septic shock or ischemic stroke.
source: In future studies, it will be interesting to test the effect of apoA1 or CyD infusion in pre-clinical models of ischemia reperfusion injury (mimicking a myocardial infarction), septic shock or ischemic stroke, all of which are situations where limiting the initial rush of inflammatory leukocytes into sites of injury could have a significant effect on subsequent tissue injury and repair processes.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications.
